processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: The different alloyed steels were produced by casting using a 100 kW vacuum induction furnace, resulting in 0.5 kg ingots (Table 1).
The ingots were hot-rolled at 1150 °C, obtaining 5 mm flat-products, followed by water quenching (parent process proc_hot-rolled-1150c of this sample).
Samples were heat treated at 600 °C and 800 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching. Only the alloys tempered at 800 °C underwent cellular transformation and/or spinodal decomposition.

structures.overall_structure: Full austenitic decomposition. γ grains followed cellular transformation into κ-carbide + α + residual-γ lamellar structures, together with spinodal decomposition; similar to 9Al-10Mn-1C (Figs. 5(a) and 6) but with κ-carbides consisting of wide, thick lath-like lamellae (Fig. 7). The Mn-γ-stabilization was balanced by the Al–C driving force for κ-carbide formation.

phases_present.morphology: wide, thick lath-like lamellae (wider and thicker than at 9% Al)
lamellar constituent of the cellular transformation product (κ-carbide + α + residual-γ lamellae)
residual γ within the κ-carbide + α + residual-γ lamellar structure

grain_structure.texture: lamellae/bands aligned along the rolling direction

phases_present.morphology: proper cuboidal morphology; the densest and thickest configuration among the alloys studied (Fig. 8(c),(d))

precipitates.distribution: homogeneously within spinodal decomposed γ grains; densest and thickest configuration of the three compositions examined

microstructure_list.region: mixed grains (δ-ferrite branches inside spinodal decomposed γ grains)

phases_present.morphology: pale, elongated branch-/dendrite-like arms penetrating the modulated matrix, linked to δ + κ-carbide lamellar grains

phases_present.crystal_structure: FCC_A1 with fine periodic cross-hatched modulation
phases_present.morphology: finely modulated matrix surrounding the δ-ferrite branches

grain_structure.texture: dark, elongated stringers/bands lying in a lighter matrix, banded along the rolling direction

interfaces.phase_evolution: γ grains underwent cellular transformation into κ-carbide + α + residual-γ lamellar structures along with spinodal decomposition of γ, giving full austenitic decomposition at 800 °C.
interfaces.interface_notes: Some grains feature a mixed structure in which δ-ferrite branches (linked to δ + κ-carbide lamellar grains) are extended inside spinodal decomposed γ grains; the paper states that this phenomenon requires further studies in order to be properly understood.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers macro-hardness (Vickers method), 5 kg load applied for all indentations, 5 indentations per sample; 800 °C — Tempered condition (Table 5)

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: Vickers hardness (HV): 357 (hot-rolled) → 404 (800 °C tempered). The 800 °C tempering produced the largest hardness gain among the four compositions tempered at 800 °C (9Al-10Mn-1C 273→356, 12Al-10Mn-1C 401→399, 12Al-20Mn-1C 357→404, 12Al-30Mn1C 324→352) and the highest tempered hardness (404 HV) of that series.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Through-thickness embedding, grinding and polishing performed separately for hot-rolled and heat-treated samples
characterization_methods.purpose: Microstructural analysis of the alloys at the different processing conditions (hot-rolling and tempering)
characterization_methods.key_findings: Optical micrograph of the 800 °C tempered 12Al-20Mn-1C (Fig. 5(c)) shows dark elongated stringers/bands lying in a lighter matrix; banded structure elongated along the rolling direction.

characterization_methods.technique: Scanning Electron Microscopy (Secondary Electron Imaging, SEI)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: SEM analysis performed only on selected microstructures; Fig. 5(c) 20kV ×2,500 10 µm bar; Fig. 7 20kV ×5,000 5 µm bar
characterization_methods.purpose: Analyse phase morphologies of the tempered microstructures
characterization_methods.key_findings: Fig. 5(c): lamellar cells emanating from a boundary next to a smoother, finely modulated region; Fig. 7: wide, thick lath-like bright κ-carbide lamellae in a darker matrix with small dark elongated pits, plus a brighter upper-left region with fine cross-hatched modulated texture.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Qualitative local phase composition; Table 7 for δ, γ and k phases
characterization_methods.purpose: Provide qualitative information on the local phase composition (Al and Mn partitioning)
characterization_methods.key_findings: Table 7 'EDS for Al and Mn in 12Al-20Mn-1C tempered at 800 °C' (wt%, Min/Mean/Max): Al δ 11.0/11.9/13.6, γ 5.7/7.8/9.9, k 10.3/10.8/11.9; Mn δ 15.2/17.9/20.8, γ 20.3/23.6/27.6, k 21.9/23.9/25.5. EDS was more accurate for this alloy because of the wide, thick κ-carbide laths.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: 5 kg load for all indentations; 5 indentations per sample; Minitab18® used to verify data consistency, outliers excluded
characterization_methods.purpose: Macro-hardness measurement to highlight chemical composition and process effects
characterization_methods.key_findings: 12Al-20Mn-1C: 357 HV hot-rolled → 404 HV after 800 °C tempering (Table 5), the largest gain of the 800 °C series.

characterization_methods.technique: CALPHAD thermodynamic equilibrium calculation (phase volume fraction / amount of all phases vs temperature)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Equilibrium amount of all phases [mol] vs temperature [°C] (0–1300 °C) for the 12Al-20Mn-1C composition (Fig. 12(c))
characterization_methods.purpose: Assess the thermodynamic gradients for austenite stability between hot-rolling (1150 °C) and tempering (800 °C)
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 12Al alloys (Fig. 12(c),(d)) the situation is reversed relative to the 9Al alloys: the austenite (FCC_A1) fraction is lower at 800 °C than at 1150 °C, which the paper links to the propensity of the 12Al alloys to transform during tempering.

computational_details.simulation_method: CALPHAD thermodynamic equilibrium calculation (equilibrium phase amount vs temperature)
computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: 12Al-20Mn-1C (Fe–Mn–Al–C) composition; equilibrium amount of all phases [mol] plotted against temperature [°C] (0–1300 °C), panel (c) of Fig. 12
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: The diagrams are used only as an indicative/qualitative indication of possible austenite transformation, because the hot-rolled condition at 1150 °C is not an equilibrium state; they are compared with the observed transformation behaviour (no transformation at 800 °C for 9Al-10Mn-0.4C vs transformation of the 12Al alloys).

analytical_models.equation_role: Equilibrium phase amounts used as a qualitative thermodynamic indicator of austenite (FCC_A1) stability and of the propensity of γ to transform during tempering
analytical_models.model_note: In the 12Al alloys the thermodynamic gradient between hot-rolling (1150 °C) and tempering (800 °C) equilibria is increased by the higher Al content; the austenite fraction is lower at 800 °C than at 1150 °C for 12Al-20/30Mn-1C, the reverse of the 9Al alloys.

unmapped_findings: Table 7 (b0056): EDS for Al and Mn in 12Al-20Mn-1C tempered at 800 °C (wt%, Min/Mean/Max). Al: δ 11.0/11.9/13.6, γ 5.7/7.8/9.9, k 10.3/10.8/11.9. Mn: δ 15.2/17.9/20.8, γ 20.3/23.6/27.6, k 21.9/23.9/25.5. Al is highest in δ-ferrite and lowest in γ; Mn is lowest in δ and highest in γ and k.

For the 12Al-20Mn-1C alloy tempered at 800 °C the cellular-transformed fractions were reported as predominant over the spinodal decomposed fractions, attributed to lower Mn-γ stability (text b0113, Fig. 13(b)); Fig. 13 was captioned for panels (a) 9Al-10Mn-1C, (b) 12Al-20Mn-1C and (c) 12Al-30Mn-1C but only the panel containing 9Al-10Mn-1C was supplied.

Internal inconsistency in the paper regarding the nano-sized κ-carbide morphology of 12Al-20Mn-1C at 800 °C: the Results text (b0057) and Fig. 8(c,d) assign the 'densest and thickest configuration with proper cuboidal morphology' to 12Al-20Mn-1C, whereas the Conclusions (b0121/b0122) attribute 'medium dense and thin needle-like κ-carbides' to 12Al + 20Mn and the 'most dense and thickest nano-sized cuboidal κ-carbides' to 12Al + 30Mn.

The inter-lamellar spacing of the 800 °C tempered 12Al-20Mn-1C structure is described only qualitatively as high/wide (b0053), stated to be consistent with the hardening effects despite the high spacing; Table 9 lists 'Wide' inter-lamellar spacing for 12Al-10Mn-1C at 800 °C (401 → 399 HV), not for this sample.

No tensile, ductility, density, thermal, electrical or magnetic property data are reported specifically for the 12Al-20Mn-1C 800 °C tempered sample; the reported mechanical data are Vickers macro-hardness only.

The paper notes (b0114) that higher hardness is related to higher tensile properties and that thick precipitates formed by spinodal decomposition are associated with brittleness, but no tensile/ductility values are given for this sample.

Fig. 7 caption (b0052) labels the product as 'κ + γ Lamellae in 12Al-20Mn-1C at 800 °C', while the citing text describes the same structure as κ-carbide + α + residual-γ lamellae produced by cellular transformation plus spinodal decomposition.
